notes.definition: Inherited disorders are conditions caused by inheriting certain alleles. Polydactyly (extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele and cystic fibrosis (a disorder of cell membranes) is caused by a recessive allele. Embryos can be screened for these alleles, which raises economic, social and ethical issues.
explanation: Some disorders are inherited: they are passed from parents to children in their genes. They are caused by the inheritance of certain alleles. Whether a person is affected depends on whether the allele causing the disorder is dominant or recessive.

Polydactyly is having extra fingers or toes. It is caused by a dominant allele, so a person needs only one copy of the allele to have the condition. Anyone with the allele shows the disorder, so it cannot be 'hidden' in carriers. If one parent is heterozygous (Dd) and the other is unaffected (dd), each child has a 1 in 2 (50%) chance of inheriting polydactyly. The extra digits are often removed by surgery, and the condition is not usually harmful.

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a disorder of cell membranes. It causes the body to produce a lot of thick, sticky mucus in the lungs and the digestive system, leading to breathing difficulties, frequent lung infections and problems digesting food. It is caused by a recessive allele, so a person must inherit two copies (ff) to have the disorder. People with one copy (Ff) do not have CF but are carriers: they can pass the allele on. If both parents are carriers (Ff × Ff), each child has a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of having CF and a 1 in 2 (50%) chance of being a carrier. There is no cure, but treatments such as physiotherapy, antibiotics and newer drugs help.

Human embryos can be screened for the alleles that cause these and other disorders. In one method, eggs are fertilised by in vitro fertilisation (IVF); when the embryos are about eight cells, one cell is removed and its DNA tested. Only embryos without the faulty alleles are implanted into the uterus. Cells from a developing fetus can also be tested during pregnancy. If the fetus has a serious disorder, parents may face the decision of whether to end the pregnancy.

Embryo screening raises economic, social and ethical issues. Economic: screening is expensive, but it may cost less than a lifetime of treatment and care for a person with a disorder. Social and ethical: screening may reduce suffering, but some people think it is wrong to destroy embryos or to end a pregnancy, and worry that it could lead to 'designer babies' chosen for desirable features rather than to avoid disease. Others feel it implies that people living with disorders are less valued. Tests are not always accurate, and a false result could lead to the wrong decision. Gene therapy, in which a working allele is put into a patient's cells, is being researched; it may alleviate suffering but also raises ethical issues, especially if changes could be passed on to future generations. You should be able to make informed judgements about these issues using data provided.
keyFacts: Some disorders are inherited and are caused by the inheritance of certain alleles.
Polydactyly (extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele.
Cystic fibrosis is a disorder of cell membranes caused by a recessive allele.
A person needs two recessive alleles (ff) to have cystic fibrosis; Ff people are carriers.
Two carrier parents: 25% chance of a child with CF, 50% chance of a carrier child.
One heterozygous parent with polydactyly and one unaffected parent: 50% chance of polydactyly.
Human embryos can be screened for the alleles that cause these and other disorders.
Embryo screening and gene therapy may alleviate suffering but raise ethical issues.
Issues to weigh up include cost, destroying embryos, 'designer babies', accuracy and how society views people with disorders.

keyTerms.definition: A condition caused by inheriting certain alleles from one or both parents.
Having extra fingers or toes; caused by a dominant allele.
A disorder of cell membranes, caused by a recessive allele, that leads to thick, sticky mucus in the lungs and digestive system.
A person who is heterozygous for a recessive allele that causes a disorder; they do not have the disorder but can pass on the allele.
Testing the DNA of an embryo (or fetus) to find out whether it has alleles that cause a genetic disorder.
A treatment, still largely being researched, that aims to put a working copy of an allele into a person's cells to treat a genetic disorder.
In vitro fertilisation: fertilising eggs with sperm outside the body, in a laboratory.

workedExamples.title: Probability of cystic fibrosis
workedExamples.question: Two parents are both carriers of cystic fibrosis. What is the probability that their child will (a) have cystic fibrosis (b) be a carrier?
steps: Carriers are Ff. Gametes from each parent: F or f.
Punnett square: FF, Ff, Ff, ff.

workedExamples.title: Probability of polydactyly
workedExamples.question: A father with polydactyly (Dd) and a mother without polydactyly (dd) have a child. What is the probability that the child has polydactyly?
steps: Gametes: father D or d; mother d only.
Punnett square: Dd, Dd, dd, dd.
Dd children have polydactyly because the allele is dominant: 2 out of 4.

workedExamples.title: Using cost data in an evaluation
workedExamples.question: Screening 10 000 embryos costs £2 000 000 and finds 4 embryos with cystic fibrosis. The lifetime cost of treating one person with CF is estimated at £600 000. Compare the costs.
steps: Use this as one point in a judgement, alongside ethical and social points.
workedExamples.answer: Screening costs £400 000 less than lifetime treatment in this example, but cost is only one factor in the decision.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think carriers of cystic fibrosis have a mild form of the disorder.
misconceptions.right: In fact carriers (Ff) do not have cystic fibrosis at all; the dominant normal allele is expressed. They can pass the recessive allele on.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think dominant disorders like polydactyly must be common.
misconceptions.right: In fact dominant means only one copy is needed to be affected. Polydactyly is still relatively rare.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think cystic fibrosis is caught from someone else.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is an inherited disorder caused by alleles; it is not infectious.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that if two carriers have one child with CF, their next three children will not have it.
misconceptions.right: In fact each child has a 1 in 4 chance, independently of their brothers and sisters.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think unaffected parents cannot have a child with an inherited disorder.
misconceptions.right: In fact two unaffected carriers of a recessive allele can have an affected child.

realWorld: In the UK, newborn babies are offered a heel prick blood test that screens for cystic fibrosis and other conditions, so treatment can start early.
Couples with a family history of a serious inherited disorder can use IVF with embryo screening so that only embryos without the faulty alleles are implanted.
New drugs for cystic fibrosis target the faulty membrane protein and have greatly improved breathing for many patients.
examTips: Learn which allele causes which disorder: polydactyly is dominant, cystic fibrosis is recessive. Swapping them is a very common error.
For cystic fibrosis, describe it as 'a disorder of cell membranes' as in the specification, then add the effect (thick, sticky mucus).
In ethics questions give arguments for and against, using economic, social and ethical points, and finish with a justified conclusion.
Use data given in the question (costs, numbers of embryos, accuracy of tests) in your answer; do not just give opinions.
Write probabilities in the form the question asks for, and remember each pregnancy is independent.
summary: Inherited disorders are caused by inheriting certain alleles.
Polydactyly: extra fingers or toes, caused by a dominant allele.
Cystic fibrosis: disorder of cell membranes, caused by a recessive allele.
Carriers are heterozygous and unaffected but can pass on a recessive allele.
Embryos can be screened for disorder alleles.
Screening and gene therapy may reduce suffering but raise economic, social and ethical issues.

questions.question: What is polydactyly?
markScheme: 1 mark: having extra fingers or toes
questions.explanation: Polydactyly means extra digits. A disorder of cell membranes describes cystic fibrosis.

questions.question: What type of allele causes cystic fibrosis?
options: It is not caused by an allele
markScheme: 1 mark: recessive
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele, so two copies are needed.

questions.question: What type of allele causes polydactyly?
options: Neither, it is caused by a virus
Only alleles on the sex chromosomes
markScheme: 1 mark: dominant
questions.explanation: Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele, so one copy is enough.

questions.question: Cystic fibrosis is a disorder of which part of the cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: cell membranes
questions.explanation: The specification describes cystic fibrosis as a disorder of cell membranes. Human cells have no cell wall.

questions.question: A person has the genotype Ff for cystic fibrosis (f is the recessive CF allele). Which describes them?
options: They have a mild form of cystic fibrosis
They are a carrier and do not have cystic fibrosis
They cannot pass on the CF allele
markScheme: 1 mark: they are a carrier and do not have cystic fibrosis
questions.explanation: The dominant F allele is expressed, so they are unaffected, but they carry f and can pass it on.

questions.question: Two parents are both carriers of cystic fibrosis. What is the probability that their child will have cystic fibrosis?
markScheme: 1 mark: 25%
questions.explanation: Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Only ff has CF, so 1 in 4 = 25%. 50% is the chance of a carrier.

questions.question: A man has polydactyly and is heterozygous (Dd). His partner does not have polydactyly. What is the chance their child will have polydactyly?
markScheme: 1 mark: 50%
questions.explanation: Dd × dd gives Dd, Dd, dd, dd. Dd has polydactyly because the allele is dominant: 2 out of 4 = 50%.

questions.question: Which of these is an ethical objection to embryo screening?
options: Embryos with the faulty allele are destroyed
Screening can be done during IVF
Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele
markScheme: 1 mark: embryos with the faulty allele are destroyed
questions.explanation: Some people believe embryos have a right to life, so destroying them is wrong. Cost is an economic issue, and the other two statements are facts, not objections.

questions.question: Two parents do not have polydactyly. What is the probability that their child will have polydactyly (assuming no new mutation)?
markScheme: 1 mark: 0
questions.explanation: Polydactyly is dominant, so unaffected parents must both be dd. They can only pass on d, so no child can inherit the D allele.

questions.question: Why can cystic fibrosis 'skip' a generation, appearing in a child when neither parent has it?
options: The allele is dominant and is sometimes hidden
The child's cells divide by meiosis
Cystic fibrosis is caused by an infection in the child
Both parents can be carriers of the recessive allele and each pass it on
markScheme: 1 mark: both parents can be carriers of the recessive allele and each pass it on
questions.explanation: Carriers (Ff) are unaffected. If both pass on f, the child is ff and has CF. A dominant allele cannot be hidden, so dominant disorders do not skip generations in this way.

questions.question: Name one inherited disorder caused by a dominant allele.
markScheme: 1 mark: polydactyly
questions.explanation: Polydactyly is the dominant disorder named in the specification.

questions.question: Describe the effects of cystic fibrosis on the body.
markScheme: 1 mark: thick, sticky mucus is produced
1 mark: in the lungs (causing breathing difficulties or infections) / in the digestive system (causing difficulty digesting food)
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is a disorder of cell membranes; the result is very thick, sticky mucus that blocks airways and digestive ducts.

questions.question: Explain why a person can be a carrier of cystic fibrosis but cannot be a carrier of polydactyly.
markScheme: 1 mark: cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele, so a heterozygous person is unaffected but carries it
1 mark: polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele, so anyone with one copy has the condition
questions.explanation: A carrier has an allele that is not expressed. That only happens with recessive alleles.

questions.question: Give one economic argument for and one economic argument against screening embryos for cystic fibrosis.
markScheme: 1 mark: for: may cost less than a lifetime of treatment and care for people with cystic fibrosis
1 mark: against: screening (and IVF) is expensive / money could be spent on other treatments
questions.explanation: Economic issues are about money. Ethical points such as destroying embryos are a different type of issue.

questions.question: Give two social or ethical concerns about embryo screening.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: embryos are destroyed (some believe they have a right to life); could lead to designer babies chosen for desirable features; suggests people living with disorders are less valued; tests may give false results; who decides which disorders to screen for
questions.explanation: These are the main concerns raised; good answers explain why each is a concern.

questions.question: A couple have a child with cystic fibrosis, although neither parent has the disorder. Explain, using a genetic diagram or clear reasoning, the parents' genotypes and the probability that their next child will be a carrier.
markScheme: 1 mark: child has CF so is ff, receiving f from each parent
1 mark: parents are unaffected so must both be Ff (carriers)
1 mark: Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff, so probability of a carrier = 2/4 = 50%
questions.explanation: Deduce the genotypes from the affected child, then use the Punnett square. Carriers are Ff only, so 2 of the 4 outcomes.

questions.question: Gene therapy for cystic fibrosis aims to put working alleles into the cells lining the lungs. Suggest one benefit and one concern about gene therapy.
markScheme: 1 mark: benefit: could alleviate suffering / treat the cause rather than the symptoms / improve quality of life
1 mark: concern: long-term effects or safety unknown / expensive / ethical issues, especially if changes could be passed on to offspring
questions.explanation: The specification states that gene therapy may alleviate suffering but raises ethical issues.

questions.question: Two carriers of cystic fibrosis have children. Give the percentage chance that a child will be a carrier.
markScheme: 1 mark: 50%
questions.explanation: Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Two out of four are Ff carriers: 50%.

questions.question: A man with polydactyly (Dd) and a woman without polydactyly (dd) have four children. How many of the children would you expect to have polydactyly?
markScheme: 1 mark: probability = 1/2
questions.explanation: Dd × dd gives a 1 : 1 ratio. Half of 4 is 2. This is only the expected number; the actual number could differ because each child is a chance event.

questions.question: About 1 in 25 people in the UK is a carrier of cystic fibrosis. In a town of 50 000 people, how many people would be expected to be carriers?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2000

questions.question: A screening programme tests 8000 embryos for an inherited disorder at a cost of £350 per test. Five affected embryos are found. The lifetime cost of care for one person with the disorder is £500 000. Calculate the difference between the total cost of the screening programme and the total lifetime cost of care for five people.
markScheme: 1 mark: screening cost = 8000 × £350 = £2 800 000 and care cost = 5 × £500 000 = £2 500 000
1 mark: difference = £2 800 000 − £2 500 000 = £300 000 (screening costs more)
questions.explanation: Screening: 8000 × 350 = £2 800 000. Care: 5 × 500 000 = £2 500 000. In this example the screening actually costs £300 000 more than the care, so on cost alone screening is not cheaper here. Always check which is bigger rather than assuming.

questions.question: Two carriers of cystic fibrosis plan to have a child. Their child does not have cystic fibrosis. What is the probability that this child is a carrier? Give your answer as a decimal to 2 decimal places.
markScheme: 1 mark: unaffected children are FF, Ff, Ff (3 outcomes)
questions.explanation: Once we know the child is unaffected, the ff outcome is excluded. Of the three remaining equally likely outcomes, two are Ff, so 2/3 = 0.67.

questions.question: Compare how polydactyly and cystic fibrosis are inherited.
markScheme: Indicative content: both are inherited disorders caused by inheriting certain alleles; polydactyly caused by a dominant allele, cystic fibrosis by a recessive allele; one copy of the polydactyly allele causes the condition (DD or Dd), two copies of the CF allele are needed (ff); people can be carriers of CF (Ff) but not of polydactyly; CF can appear in children of two unaffected parents, polydactyly needs at least one affected parent; Dd × dd gives 50% chance of polydactyly, Ff × Ff gives 25% chance of CF; polydactyly is extra fingers or toes, CF is a disorder of cell membranes.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison including dominant versus recessive and its consequences (carriers, number of copies or probabilities).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or both disorders with little comparison.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The central difference is dominant versus recessive. Good answers then follow through the consequences: carriers, number of copies needed and probabilities.

questions.question:
A couple who are both carriers of cystic fibrosis are considering IVF with embryo screening.
Evaluate the use of embryo screening for this couple. Include economic, social and ethical issues and give a justified conclusion.
markScheme: Indicative content. Biology: both Ff, each child has a 25% chance of CF; screening identifies ff embryos so only unaffected embryos are implanted. For: prevents a child suffering from CF (breathing problems, infections, shortened life); reduces emotional stress for parents; may reduce the long-term cost of treatment and care to the NHS; parents can make an informed choice; avoids possible later decision about ending a pregnancy. Against: embryos with CF (and possibly unused embryos) are destroyed, which some believe is wrong because embryos have a right to life; IVF and screening are expensive and IVF success rates are not high; removing a cell carries a small risk; tests may not be completely accurate; could lead to screening for non-medical features (designer babies); may suggest people with CF are less valued; carriers (Ff) would still be implanted and could pass on the allele. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement, for example that screening is justified for a serious disorder like CF because it reduces suffering, while recognising ethical objections.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): balanced evaluation with economic, social and ethical arguments for and against, linked to the couple's situation, with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): arguments for and against with some reference to at least two types of issue; conclusion may be weak or missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two simple points, mainly one-sided.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Evaluate means weigh up both sides and come to a judgement. Using the 25% figure and the specific effects of CF shows biological understanding as well as ethical reasoning.

questions.question: State what is meant by an inherited disorder.
acceptedAnswers: passed on in genes from parents
markScheme: 1 mark: a disorder caused by the inheritance of certain alleles (passed on from parents)
questions.explanation: Inherited disorders are passed on through alleles, unlike communicable diseases, which are caused by pathogens.

questions.question: Embryos produced by IVF can be screened. What happens to the embryos found to have no alleles for the disorder?
options: They can be implanted into the mother's uterus
They are frozen and never used
markScheme: 1 mark: they can be implanted into the mother's uterus
questions.explanation: The purpose of screening is to choose embryos without the faulty alleles for implantation.
